Apple has filed documents regarding App Store external transaction commissions in the Epic Games lawsuit. Details below.

Apple files App Store external transaction commission proposal

After repeatedly requesting a stay on district court proceedings—which will determine how and whether Apple can collect commissions on transactions made within the App Store but outside its IAP system—Apple has finally filed its proposal outlining a suggested fee structure.

Apple filed the proposal shortly after the Supreme Court denied its request to stay the lower court proceedings. Apple had hoped to stay the proceedings pending Supreme Court review of its case; if granted, Apple might have been found in contempt for charging a 27% commission on App Store external transactions. Earlier, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers had issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to direct users to alternative purchase methods.

Apple had argued at both the district court and subsequently the Supreme Court that the court's ruling could affect the outcome of the fee determination proceedings, and that the proceedings should therefore be stayed pending the court's decision. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's request, allowing the district court proceedings to continue during the pendency of the appeal.

Accordingly, Apple has now filed its proposal, suggesting the following fees:

Standard apps charged at 15% (such apps currently pay a 30% in-app purchase ("IAP") commission);

Apple stated: "The relevant factual and expert evidence regarding the proposed commission rates has also been submitted concurrently." The company added:

Apple further noted that its "proposed external link commission is also comparable to commissions charged by other competing app stores," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also noted: "The standard external link fee structure for the Google Play Store is: standard rate 20%, program rate 15%, subscription rate 10%—rates which Epic has also agreed to."

Apple stated that it still believes the fee determination proceedings should be stayed pending the outcome of the Supreme Court case, and added that the submission of this proposal is purely in compliance with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also noted that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's blanket injunction on external link transaction commissions, stating that such commissions only become problematic if they effectively amount to a prohibition.

Following Apple's filing, Epic may now respond, and Apple is expected to submit its brief to the Supreme Court by September 14.
